q-1777484902494:
I want to work at DALI because I am looking for a place where I can build useful things while feeling more connected to the engineering and design community at Dartmouth. In other projects, I have learned that it is easy to study a field from the outside and understand its tools, but still feel separate from the actual craft. DALI seems like the kind of place where I can learn by doing, work around people who care about design and its community, and build the confidence that comes from contributing to projects.

I also have friends and mentors involved in DALI, and it would mean a lot to join that community and contribute alongside them. What draws me to DALI is that its projects are not only technically creative, but often socially thoughtful. Projects like Evergreen show that DALI uses its resources to solve problems that matter, and that is the kind of environment I want to be part of.
q-1777484932060:
Around 16 when I first moved out, I decided to build a custom motorcycle from an old 1984 Kawasaki KZ550. I have been interested in motorcycles since I was young, grew up riding dirt bikes, and still ride daily, so this project felt like a long time dream. I was inspired by YouTube builders and motorcycle forums, and as I worked on the bike, I started to feel more connected to those communities. I loved that the project combined mechanical problem solving with a culture I already cared about.

The hardest part was sourcing parts for an older machine. I could not find the right airbox and intake components, which were critical for getting the engine to run. I eventually worked around this by manufacturing my own parts with help from an aerospace engineer neighbor who had a CNC lathe in his garage. I also learned older repair tricks, like making gaskets by hand, which made me appreciate the bike even more. The project was difficult because I did not have the proper lifts, tools, or replacement parts, but that forced me to be resourceful.
q-1777484937765:
Over the last term, I worked on a mathematical finance research project focused on detecting fast dynamics in the pricing of short time to expiry options. I worked with people who had strengths in areas where I was still learning, including mathematics, data visualization, data pipelines, and repository management. I wrote over 6,000 lines of Python during the term, but the project became much stronger because of the feedback and help from my teammates. I especially enjoyed building a workflow that felt close to industry, where we had to clean messy data, test ideas, and find creative ways to estimate things we could not observe directly, such as using butterfly spreads to estimate curvature. Using the libraries bloomberg data terminals was also new and very exciting to me with this project!

One thing that could have been better was our communication structure. We all worked at different times of day and in different work styles, so it was sometimes hard to move quickly when we were waiting on each other. About halfway through, we fixed this by setting clearer meeting times, creating a shared board of remaining tasks, and sending weekly project updates. Those changes made the team more organized and helped us finish stronger. I wish we had set that structure earlier, but it taught me a lot about what good collaboration needs before the technical work starts.
